quick_warnings: Mérida airport (MID) is ~2 hours west; Cancún (CUN) is ~2 hours east — choose based on your itinerary.
Heat and humidity are intense May–Sep; carry water and plan cenote visits for midday relief.
Chichén Itzá is only 40 min away but gets crowded after 10 AM — go at opening for the best experience.

detail_guide.getting_around: Valladolid is a compact colonial town easily explored on foot or by bicycle. Colectivos run to nearby cenotes and Chichén Itzá. ADO buses connect to Mérida and Cancún. Taxis are inexpensive for short trips around town.

top_sights.name: Cenote Zací
top_sights.description: A large open cenote right in the center of town with a cave overhang, stalactites, and swimming access.

top_sights.name: Convento de San Bernardino de Siena
top_sights.description: One of the oldest churches in the Yucatán (1552), with a monastery, gardens, and a light show at night.

top_sights.name: Cenote Suytún
top_sights.description: A photogenic underground cenote with a circular stone platform and a beam of light piercing through the ceiling.

museums.name: Museo de San Roque
museums.description: Small museum in a former church chronicling Valladolid's colonial history and the Caste War of Yucatán.

parks.name: Parque Francisco Cantón Rosado
parks.description: The main plaza surrounded by colorful colonial buildings, the cathedral, and vendors selling local snacks.

eat_drink_work.name: Bazar Municipal
eat_drink_work.description: Covered market on the main plaza serving authentic Yucatecan dishes like salbutes, panuchos, and lomitos.

eat_drink_work.name: Yerbabuena del Sisal
eat_drink_work.description: Garden restaurant in a colonial courtyard with creative takes on Yucatecan cuisine and craft mezcal.

eat_drink_work.name: Squimz Cafe
eat_drink_work.description: Bright cafe with good espresso, smoothies, and Wi-Fi — a reliable spot for digital nomads.
